## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Rurumigarājajātaka* (Ja 482) is a Jātaka tale whose introductory narrative is set while the Buddha was dwelling at the Bamboo-grove (*Veḷuvana*) [SuttaCentral]. It was delivered regarding Devadatta, who claimed that the Buddha had done him no good whatever, maintaining that he had received ordination, learned the Three Baskets, and gained honor entirely through his own agency [SuttaCentral]. In response to the monks discussing Devadatta's ingratitude in the Hall of Truth, the Buddha revealed that Devadatta had also shown gross ingratitude in a former existence after the Bodhisatta had saved his life [SuttaCentral]. In Pali exegesis, the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* cites the Bodhisatta's birth as the Ruru deer king (*Rūrūmigarāja*) as an illustrative example of the supreme perfection of patience, specifically endurance-patience (*adhivāsanakkhanti*) [Endo 1997].
Textual reuse data computed by DharmaNexus indicates significant internal Pali parallels between this Jātaka and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* as well as the *Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Across non-Pali corpora, DharmaNexus identifies passages aligned with Kṣemendra's *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* (Tibetan D4155-2), the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu*, the Tibetan *Damamūka* (D0341), and the *Ārya-aṅgulimālīya-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra* (Tibetan D0213) [DharmaNexus].
